# Singularities and contour integrals

Laurent series classify isolated singularities and determine contour integrals around poles.

## Exercises

### Singularities

::: {#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-consider-function-how-many-poles-does recommended="math" level="intermediate"}

Consider the function $f(z) = \frac{1}{z(z-1)}$. How many poles does $f$ have, and where are they? What are the order of the poles? Can you write down the Laurent series of $f$ around $z=0$?

:::

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-does-function-have-pole-where-order}

Does the function $f(z) = 1/\sin(z)$ have a pole? Where? What order?

:::

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-find-singularities}

Find the singularities of $f(z) = e^{-1/(z-1)^2}$.

:::

### Line integrals

Let

$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{z^3-(2+\mathrm{i})z^2+(1+2\mathrm{i})z-\mathrm{i}}.
$$

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-simple-closed-curve-defined-counter-clockwise}

Let $\Gamma_\epsilon(w)$ be the simple closed curve defined by the counter-clockwise border of the $\epsilon$-ball $B_\epsilon(w)$. Write down a parameterization (a path) for this curve.

:::

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-identify-poles-their-order-hint-zero}

Identify the poles $P = \{w_1, w_2, \cdots \}$ of $f(z)$ and their order. Hint: A zero of the denominator is $z = \mathrm{i}$.

:::

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-value-around-origin}

What is the value of $$\oint_{\Gamma_\epsilon(0)} f(z)\, \mathrm{d}z$$ for $\epsilon = 1/2$?

:::

:::{#exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-find-value-line-integrals-hint-don}

Find the value of the line integrals $$\oint_{\Gamma_\epsilon(w_i)} f(z) \, \mathrm{d}z$$ for $\epsilon=1/2$. Hint: Do not attempt the integral directly; compute the relevant Laurent coefficient. It can be useful to use the Taylor expansion $$\frac{1}{a - z} = \frac{1}{a} \frac{1}{1 - z/a} = \frac{1}{a} \sum_{n=0}^\infty (z/a)^n.$$

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="tutor"}

## Solutions

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-consider-function-how-many-poles-does {.unnumbered}

The poles are simple and occur at $z=0$ and $z=1$. For $0<|z|<1$,

$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{z(z-1)}
=-\frac{1}{z(1-z)}
=-z^{-1}-1-z-z^2-\cdots.
$$

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-does-function-have-pole-where-order {.unnumbered}

The zeros of $\sin z$ occur at $z=k\pi$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and each zero is simple because $\cos(k\pi)=(-1)^k\neq0$. Thus $1/\sin z$ has a simple pole at every $k\pi$. Near the origin, $1/\sin z\sim1/z$.

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-find-singularities {.unnumbered}

The exponent has a pole at $z=1$ (of order 2). This means that the exponential function gives an essential singularity at $z=1$.

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-simple-closed-curve-defined-counter-clockwise {.unnumbered}

$\gamma(t) = w + \epsilon e^{it}$, $0 \leq t < 2\pi$.

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-identify-poles-their-order-hint-zero {.unnumbered}

The denominator can be factorized as $(z-1)^2(z-\mathrm{i})$, and therefore we have a pole of order 2 at $w_1 = 1$ and a pole of order 1 at $w_2 = \mathrm{i}$.

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-value-around-origin {.unnumbered}

The function has no poles inside the $\epsilon$-ball, so the integral is zero by Cauchy's integral theorem.

### Solution to @exr-singularities-and-contour-integrals-find-value-line-integrals-hint-don {.unnumbered}

Since

$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{(z-1)^2(z-\mathrm{i})},
$$

the residue at the second-order pole $z=1$ is

$$
\operatorname{Res}(f,1)
=\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\frac{1}{z-\mathrm{i}}\right|_{z=1}
=-\frac{1}{(1-\mathrm{i})^2}
=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}.
$$

The residue at the simple pole $z=\mathrm{i}$ is

$$
\operatorname{Res}(f,\mathrm{i})
=\frac{1}{(\mathrm{i}-1)^2}
=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\oint_{\Gamma_{1/2}(1)}f(z)\,\mathrm{d}z=\pi,
\qquad
\oint_{\Gamma_{1/2}(\mathrm{i})}f(z)\,\mathrm{d}z=-\pi.
$$

:::
